transcript:
HEADER: 2026-03-29 14:00 PDT | Duration: 42m | Attendees: Alex Chen, Priya Kapoor (Redwood); Sarah Nguyen, Ethan Park, Maya Patel (Bluecrest)

SUMMARY SECTION (auto-generated, may be rough): Redwood demo focuses on org/project keys and rate-limits; customer asks about per-tenant quotas, how 429s are surfaced, and security controls. Next steps to provision trial org and run benchmarks.

00:00 Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we are excited to show how Redwood handles rate limits and multi-tenant controls, I'm Alex, I'm the AE on this account.
00:07 Sarah Nguyen: thanks Alex, quick context — we're exploring hosted inference for our clinical notes summarization pipeline, want tight per-project isolation and predictable throttling so our downstream services don't blow up.
00:15 Priya Kapoor: awesome, thanks Sarah. I'll share my screen and jump into the Console to show org keys, project keys, per-project quotas, and example API calls. bear with me while i switch screens.
00:30 Priya Kapoor: ok screen's up — this is the Redwood Console. at the top you can see Organization settings, Projects, Keys, and Observability. i'll click Projects.
00:40 Ethan Park: quick q: when you say project, is that like a tenant id? we run multiple internal teams and a SaaS tenant per customer.
00:48 Priya Kapoor: yes, you can map projects to either internal teams or tenant ids — projects are the unit for billing, quotas, and keys. you can create project keys scoped to a project and different roles.
01:02 Priya Kapoor: creating a project now — "bluecrest-realtime" — done. next i go to Keys -> Create Key -> choose type: org key or project key. org keys are high-level and can access multiple projects, project keys are scoped.
01:20 Maya Patel: for security we prefer project keys so a compromised key only affects one project. do you support key rotation and granular expiry?
01:28 Alex Chen: yes rotation, short-lived keys via our API, and we integrate with KMS for envelope encryption. we'll share the how-to in the security docs.
01:35 Priya Kapoor: demoing quota config — per-project quotas are here: daily token quota, monthly quota, and qps rate limits. you can also set burst windows and a burst capacity factor.
01:50 Priya Kapoor: i'll set a per-project QPS limit to 50 rps and a burst of 150 for short windows, and a monthly token cap. save. notice this is separate from org-wide defaults.
02:05 Ethan Park: how do you enforce rates on the API side — is it per-API key, per-IP, or per-project aggregate?
02:12 Priya Kapoor: enforcement is by project and by key. the runtime tags incoming requests with project id based on the key. we also have optional IP-level and region-level policies for stricter control.
02:24 Sarah Nguyen: what about rate-limiting behavior — do you return classic 429s? is there a retry-after? how do you handle in-flight requests during bursts?
02:33 Priya Kapoor: good question — we return 429 with Retry-After header. for streaming responses we try to drain tokens for already started generations; if we hit project-level hard cap incoming requests receive 429. you can configure soft-limits that throttle or queue for a short period instead of immediate 429.
02:55 Alex Chen: and we have canary fallback policies; for dedicated customers we can route overflow to a cheaper model variant or a lower-priority pool automatically.
03:05 Ethan Park: hmm, for us predictable latency is key. if you queue, that could increase tail lat. we prefer immediate 429 so our circuit breakers trip.
03:12 Priya Kapoor: totally — that's why we have both soft and hard policies. you choose the behavior per project.
03:18 Maya Patel: on auditability — do you log which key and project triggered a 429? we need to have that in our audit trail for compliance.
03:25 Priya Kapoor: yes all throttling events are logged with key id, project id, policy id, and timestamp. logs are exportable to S3 or a SIEM via streaming.
03:34 Sarah Nguyen: what about RBAC integration — can we make keys tied to SSO users and have limited scopes?
03:40 Alex Chen: we integrate with your IdP via SAML/SCIM. RBAC in Console lets you assign roles (Admin, Billing, Viewer, Ops) at org or project level. project keys can be issued by an operator role only.
03:52 Priya Kapoor: switching to API examples — here is a cURL where you pass x-redwood-key: <project_key> and model param. the response includes headers x-rw-remaining, x-rw-limit, and x-rw-retry-after when applicable.
04:10 Ethan Park: can those headers be disabled? we prefer not to leak quota info in some internal flows.
04:16 Priya Kapoor: yes you can toggle response headers in org settings; we also offer a metadata-only endpoint that returns quota state for monitoring without exposing in production responses.
04:26 Alex Chen: pricing note — per-project quotas help control spend; you can set token caps per project to avoid surprises.
04:33 Sarah Nguyen: curious about org keys for orchestration — we have orchestration services that need cross-project access, but they're sensitive. best practice?
04:40 Priya Kapoor: use org keys with role restrictions and rotate often, pair with IP allowlists and limited TTL. for higher security use service accounts tied to your KMS and short lived tokens via the Redwood token-exchange API.
04:54 Priya Kapoor: demoing the Optimize suggestions — Console shows recommended batch size and quantization profile per project based on typical sequence lengths, which will reduce token cost and change throughput.
05:10 Ethan Park: will that change model quality? any safety nets?
05:15 Priya Kapoor: Optimize suggests safe quantization profiles and we track quality metrics; you can autopilot or review before applying. we also tie regressions to prompt sets and will roll back if quality drops.
05:28 Maya Patel: for SOC2 we need KMS integration and proof of encryption; is that in the security doc?
05:33 Alex Chen: yes, we'll send the whitepaper and KMS integration steps in the pack.
05:40 Priya Kapoor: switching back — observability. Console shows per-project token usage over time, per-route latency percentiles, and cost breakdown. here's an example graph: you can set alerts on when a project is approaching quota.
05:59 Ethan Park: can we get syslog/Splunk export for those alerts?
06:03 Priya Kapoor: yes alerts can integrate with PagerDuty, Slack, and webhook endpoints — logs and metrics can be exported to your monitoring stack.
06:13 Sarah Nguyen: can you demo a scenario where a project hits quota and we see the downstream effect?
06:18 Priya Kapoor: sure — i'll throttle this project's QPS down to 2 and trigger a request.
06:24 Priya Kapoor: (typing) ok making API call now...
06:32 Priya Kapoor: you can see the API returned 429 and the header Retry-After: 30. the Console alerted and flagged the project as throttled.
06:40 Alex Chen: that's the hard-cap behavior. if you prefer a soft window we could have returned a 202 and queued for up to 10 seconds.
06:48 Ethan Park: good to see the behavior. one more deep question — for multi-tenant scenarios, is enforcement eventually consistent? e.g., if you have multiple frontends in different regions, how do you prevent going over a global cap?
06:59 Priya Kapoor: enforcement is global — the control plane syncs policies to regional runtimes. there is a small replication window (< 2s typical) but we account for that with burst capacity settings. for strict global absolute caps we recommend Dedicated mode with reserved pools.
07:18 Sarah Nguyen: what's the difference between Dedicated and Hosted for rate-limits?
07:22 Alex Chen: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and we can guarantee throughput SLOs with custom rate-limits and capacity to avoid cross-tenant interference. Hosted has shared pools with policy isolation; it's cheaper and quicker to spin up.
07:36 Maya Patel: any compliance constraints for data residency? our data has to stay in a specific region.
07:41 Priya Kapoor: you can pin projects to regions for data residency and we support Private deployments for full on-prem. we'll cover details in the security pack.
07:52 Ethan Park: ok could you show how to programmatically change quotas? we have an infra job that will bump quotas during release windows.
07:58 Priya Kapoor: absolutely — here's the admin API: POST /v1/admin/projects/{id}/quota with payload, you authenticate with an org admin key. here's a quick example in Python.
08:14 Priya Kapoor: note audit log is created for any change and we write an entry with user, change, and request id.
08:22 Sarah Nguyen: on billing, if a project hits monthly token cap, do you throttle or bill overage?
08:28 Alex Chen: configurable — default is to throttle at cap. you can opt-in for on-demand overages or pre-purchased committed capacity.
08:36 Maya Patel: what about per-user rate limits inside a project? we have per-customer throttling needs inside a project.
08:42 Priya Kapoor: you can implement per-user keys or we have nested policies that allow per-customer sub-quotas enforced by passing a sub-tenant header that's validated by your own middleware; deeper per-user enforcement is a common POC request.
08:58 Ethan Park: any limits on number of projects per org? we might create thousands.\09:03 Priya Kapoor: no hard cap — large customers run thousands; UI pagination and API for provisioning scale.
09:10 Sarah Nguyen: a quick question on SDKs — do SDKs automatically surface retry-after and handle backoff?
09:16 Priya Kapoor: yes our official SDKs include exponential backoff helpers and expose quota headers; you can opt to use them or roll your own.
09:24 Alex Chen: want to quickly show the segmentation between org and project keys in the UI and then we'll open it for questions?
09:30 Priya Kapoor: sure — here's the key list: you can revoke, rotate, and set TTLs. i'll create a short-lived key now to demo. created. the key has 15m TTL by default for this template.
09:44 Maya Patel: are revocations immediate? if a key is revoked will in-flight requests fail?
09:49 Priya Kapoor: revocations propagate quickly; in-flight already accepted requests will continue, but new auth attempts with the revoked key are rejected.\09:59 Ethan Park: how does metric collection impact latency — are you sampling?
10:03 Priya Kapoor: we collect request-level telemetry but sample detailed traces to avoid overhead. basic metrics (latency, status codes) are always captured.
10:14 Sarah Nguyen: for the POC we'll need a reproducible traffic generator — can Redwood provide load scripts?
10:20 Priya Kapoor: yes Priya: we have a benchmark harness and k6 scripts we can share and run together during the POC.
10:27 Alex Chen: ok let's talk runway and next steps — based on this call seems like trial org + benchmark + security review.
10:34 Sarah Nguyen: yes that's right. our timeline is two weeks to evaluate and then a decision.
10:38 Alex Chen: perfect. we'll get the trial tenant provisioned and send the security pack; Priya will own the POC run.
10:45 Maya Patel: one last nutty corner case — if you have auto-scaling in Dedicated, can you override project throttles during a hot failover? basically want an emergency override.
10:58 Priya Kapoor: we can configure emergency override roles that allow a manual bump; auto-scale behavior is managed by policy and we can have escalation playbooks integrated with PagerDuty.
11:10 Ethan Park: ok good. any limitations on the size of the Retry-After window?
11:15 Priya Kapoor: it's configurable per policy; typical windows are seconds to minutes, but you can set long windows for monthly caps.
11:23 Alex Chen: we're about halfway through the demo recording, any other questions?
11:28 Sarah Nguyen: no further questions, appreciate the walkthrough.
11:31 Priya Kapoor: wrapping up with a quick recap — showed creating project & keys, setting per-project QPS and token caps, differences between soft vs hard limits, headers returned, audit logs, and programmatic APIs. next steps — we'll provision a trial org, share security docs, and schedule a POC benchmark next week.
11:50 Alex Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with the pack.
11:55 Sarah Nguyen: thanks all.

END TRANSCRIPT (approx 42 minutes)
